final_proof:
Let all \(L^p\)-spaces below be real. We first prove the result when both measures are finite.

Put \(\lambda=\mu+\nu\). On the Hilbert space \(L^2(\lambda)\), define
\[
T(f)=\int_X f\,d\nu.
\]
This is well-defined, since \(\nu\leq\lambda\), and it is bounded: by Cauchy--Schwarz,
\[
 |T(f)|\leq \nu(X)^{1/2}\left(\int_X |f|^2\,d\nu\right)^{1/2}
 \leq \nu(X)^{1/2}\|f\|_{L^2(\lambda)}.
\]
The Riesz representation theorem therefore gives a measurable function \(h\in L^2(\lambda)\) such that
\[
 \int_X f\,d\nu=\int_X fh\,d\lambda \qquad(f\in L^2(\lambda)). \tag{1}
\]
Taking \(f=\mathbf 1_A\), which belongs to \(L^2(\lambda)\) because \(\lambda\) is finite, gives
\[
 \nu(A)=\int_A h\,d\lambda \qquad(A\in\Sigma). \tag{2}
\]
For \(A=\{h<0\}\), (2) implies that \(\int_Ah\,d\lambda\geq0\), so \(\lambda(A)=0\); indeed, a strictly negative integrable function cannot have nonnegative integral on a set of positive measure (equivalently, use the sets \(\{h\leq-1/n\}\)). Moreover, \(\nu(A)\leq\lambda(A)\) and (2) show
\[
 \int_A(h-1)\,d\lambda\leq0
\]
for every \(A\). Applying this to \(A=\{h>1\}\) shows \(h\leq1\) almost everywhere. Thus, after changing a representative on a \(\lambda\)-null set, we may suppose \(0\leq h\leq1\) everywhere.

Let \(N=\{h=1\}\). By (2),
\[
 \nu(N)=\int_Nh\,d\lambda=\lambda(N)=\mu(N)+\nu(N),
\]
and hence \(\mu(N)=0\). The hypothesis \(\nu\ll\mu\) then gives \(\nu(N)=0\), and consequently \(\lambda(N)=0\). Define the finite-valued measurable function
\[
 g(x)=
 \begin{cases}
 \dfrac{h(x)}{1-h(x)},&x\notin N,\\[5pt]
 0,&x\in N.
 \end{cases} \tag{3}
\]
Subtracting (2) from the identity \(\lambda(A)=\int_A1\,d\lambda\) yields
\[
 \mu(A)=\int_A(1-h)\,d\lambda \qquad(A\in\Sigma). \tag{4}
\]
We use the elementary consequence of (4): if a measure \(\rho\) satisfies \(\rho(A)=\int_Aw\,d\lambda\) for every measurable \(A\), then
\[
 \int_X\varphi\,d\rho=\int_X\varphi w\,d\lambda \tag{5}
\]
for every nonnegative measurable \(\varphi\). Formula (5) follows first for indicators, then for nonnegative simple functions by linearity, and finally for arbitrary nonnegative functions by monotone convergence. Applying it to (4), with \(\varphi=\mathbf1_Ag\), and using \(\lambda(N)=0\), gives
\[
 \int_Ag\,d\mu
 =\int_Ag(1-h)\,d\lambda
 =\int_Ah\,d\lambda
 =\nu(A). \tag{6}
\]
This proves existence in the finite-measure case.

Now suppose merely that \(\mu\) and \(\nu\) are sigma-finite. Choose measurable covers \((M_i)_{i\geq1}\) and \((V_j)_{j\geq1}\) of \(X\) such that \(\mu(M_i)<\infty\) and \(\nu(V_j)<\infty\). The countable family \((M_i\cap V_j)_{i,j\geq1}\) covers \(X\); enumerate it as \((C_n)_{n\geq1}\) and disjointize it by
\[
 E_1=C_1,\qquad E_n=C_n\setminus\bigcup_{k<n}C_k\quad(n\geq2).
\]
Then \((E_n)\) is a measurable partition of \(X\), and both \(\mu(E_n)\) and \(\nu(E_n)\) are finite. On the measurable space \(E_n\), apply the finite case to the restrictions of \(\mu\) and \(\nu\). Absolute continuity passes to these restrictions, so there is a nonnegative finite-valued measurable \(g_n:E_n\to[0,\infty)\) such that
\[
 \nu(A\cap E_n)=\int_{A\cap E_n}g_n\,d\mu \qquad(A\in\Sigma). \tag{7}
\]
Define \(g:X\to[0,\infty)\) by \(g=g_n\) on \(E_n\). This function is measurable because the \(E_n\)'s form a countable measurable partition and each \(g_n\) is measurable on \(E_n\). By countable additivity and the monotone convergence theorem, applied to the increasing partial sums \(\sum_{n\leq m}\mathbf1_{E_n}g_n\),
\[
 \nu(A)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\nu(A\cap E_n)
 =\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\int_{A\cap E_n}g_n\,d\mu
 =\int_Ag\,d\mu
\]
for every \(A\in\Sigma\). This proves existence in general.

For uniqueness, let \(g_1,g_2:X\to[0,\infty)\) both have the asserted property. By sigma-finiteness of \(\nu\), choose measurable \(B_m\) covering \(X\) with \(\nu(B_m)<\infty\). Set
\[
 D_m=B_m\cap\{g_1>g_2\}.
\]
Both \(g_1\) and \(g_2\) are integrable on \(D_m\), because
\[
 \int_{D_m}g_i\,d\mu=\nu(D_m)\leq\nu(B_m)<\infty.
\]
If \(\mu(D_m)>0\), then the nonnegative function \(g_1-g_2\), which is strictly positive throughout \(D_m\), has strictly positive integral there. Indeed,
\[
D_m=\bigcup_{k\geq1}\{x\in D_m:g_1(x)-g_2(x)\geq1/k\},
\]
so one of these sets would have positive measure. But
\[
 \int_{D_m}(g_1-g_2)\,d\mu
 =\nu(D_m)-\nu(D_m)=0,
\]
a contradiction. Thus every \(D_m\) is \(\mu\)-null, and since the \(B_m\)'s cover \(X\), \(\{g_1>g_2\}\) is \(\mu\)-null. Interchanging \(g_1\) and \(g_2\) shows that \(\{g_2>g_1\}\) is also \(\mu\)-null. Hence \(g_1=g_2\) \(\mu\)-almost everywhere.
